title: CAP Theorem (and PACELC)
tagline: When the network splits, you must choose: consistency or availability. The most misquoted idea in system design, done right.
summary: What CAP really says, why you can't 'give up P', and PACELC.

paragraphs: The CAP theorem concerns any distributed system that replicates data, and names three properties: **Consistency** (every read sees the latest write — like one copy), **Availability** (every request gets a non-error response), and **Partition tolerance** (the system keeps working even when the network drops/delays messages between nodes).

The theorem: when a **network partition** happens, you can have *at most two* of the three. And here's the part most people get wrong — in a distributed system, partitions *will* happen (cables fail, switches reboot, packets drop). So **P is not optional**. The real choice during a partition is binary: **CP** (sacrifice availability to stay consistent) or **AP** (stay available but serve possibly-stale data).

blocks.title: The #1 CAP misconception
blocks.text: You do NOT 'pick 2 of 3' freely. You cannot give up partition tolerance in a real distributed system — partitions are a fact of nature. CAP only forces a trade-off *during a partition*, and that trade-off is C vs A. When the network is healthy, you can have both.

sections.title: CP vs AP: the choice during a partition

blocks.caption: During a partition, node A can't reach node B. A write arrives at A. Does A reject it (CP) or accept it and reconcile later (AP)?

rows: Refuse/block requests it can't make consistent (error or wait)
Keep serving from each side; reconcile later
Possibly stale data, but always an answer
Banking, inventory, config, locks, unique IDs

blocks.text: Many modern databases are *tunable* per request — e.g., Cassandra/DynamoDB let you choose consistency level (ONE vs QUORUM vs ALL) per query. So you can be AP for a feed read and CP for a critical write in the same database.

paragraphs: CAP only talks about behaviour *during a partition*. But partitions are rare; what about the 99.99% of the time the network is fine? **PACELC** extends CAP: **if Partition (P) then choose Availability or Consistency (A/C); Else (E), choose Latency or Consistency (L/C).**

The insight: even with a healthy network, achieving strong consistency requires coordination between replicas, which *costs latency*. So every replicated system makes a second, everyday trade-off between low latency and strong consistency. For example, DynamoDB is **PA/EL** (favours availability and low latency), while a system like Spanner is **PC/EC** (favours consistency in both cases, paying latency for it).

blocks.text: Mentioning PACELC is an instant senior signal. The crisp version: 'CAP forces C-vs-A during a partition; PACELC adds that even without partitions, strong consistency costs latency, so there's always a latency-vs-consistency trade-off too.'

cheatsheet: CAP: during a network partition you get at most 2 of Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance.
P is NOT optional in a real distributed system — partitions happen. The real choice during a partition is CP vs AP.
CP = consistent but may reject requests (banking, inventory, locks). AP = always answers but may be stale (feeds, carts, likes).
Many stores (Cassandra, DynamoDB) tune consistency per request (ONE/QUORUM/ALL).
PACELC: Else (no partition) you still trade Latency vs Consistency — strong consistency costs coordination latency.

questions.prompt: Your interviewer says 'just pick CA — give up partition tolerance.' Why is that the wrong framing for a distributed system?
questions.hint: Can you choose whether the network fails?
answer: Partition tolerance isn't a feature you opt into — it's whether your system keeps functioning when the network inevitably drops or delays messages between nodes. In any system spread across machines, partitions *will* occur, so you must tolerate them. A 'CA' system only exists if everything is on a single node (no network between replicas), which isn't a distributed system.

So the honest framing is: P is assumed, and CAP only tells you what to do *when* a partition strikes — stay consistent and reject some requests (CP), or stay available and serve possibly-stale data (AP). When the network is healthy, you can have both C and A.
keyPoints: P = tolerate inevitable network failures, not optional
CA only makes sense on a single node
Real choice is CP vs AP during a partition
Both C and A are achievable when the network is healthy
followUps: What does your database do during a partition by default — does it know?

questions.prompt: You're designing a shopping cart and a payment/checkout system. Which should lean AP and which CP, and why?
questions.hint: Where is a stale/duplicate value annoying vs financially wrong?
answer: The **cart** should lean AP: users must always be able to add/remove items even during a partition. If two replicas briefly disagree, you can merge carts later (take the union of items) — a stale cart is annoying at worst, and Amazon famously chose availability here.

**Checkout/payment** should lean CP: charging a card or decrementing paid inventory must be globally agreed and correct. It's better to show 'try again in a moment' than to double-charge or oversell. So you accept reduced availability on the narrow critical write to guarantee consistency. This split — AP for the browsing/cart path, CP for the money path — is exactly how mature systems apply CAP per operation.
keyPoints: Cart = AP: always editable, merge on reconcile
Checkout = CP: correctness over availability for money
Apply CAP per operation, not system-wide
Better to fail a payment safely than double-charge
followUps: How would you 'merge' two divergent carts after a partition heals?
